At any one moment the limit's refusal (L1-10) is the same for every address, but the count it reads gains a place only when the sender reserves one for a mailed message (`backend/modules/accounts/integrations/account_mail.py:221`). Near the daily limit, a caller can therefore tell from whether the next request is refused that an earlier request's address was mailed, and a caller with a reset-required account of their own can read the same edge from the forced reset's `over_allowance` word (`backend/modules/accounts/services/first_sign_in.py:284`): about one bit per probe, at the cost of the day's 90 places. It predates L1-69 (D12, L1-10), which only delays it until the sender runs. Charging a place for an unknown address too would let anonymous requests drain the allowance with any addresses at all. Today one known address can already drain it, through the password-reset request or the forced reset, each operation a new message (`backend/modules/accounts/u8_entry.py:286`, `first_sign_in.py:233-237`); with L1-71's limit of five account emails per account a day, spending the day's 90 places takes 18 eligible addresses, and holding back digests at 60 takes 12, while registration stays closed. Around 00:00 UTC it takes fewer: the count is kept on the UTC day of the request, but a signed-out message takes its place on the day the sender delivers it (`account_mail.py:221`, `backend/modules/operations/allowance.py:40-42`), so messages asked for just before 00:00 UTC and sent after it take the new day's places while they count on the old day's, and around 09:00 in Seoul one address can take up to 10 of one day's places: about 9 eligible addresses, or 6 to hold back digests. Once public activation opens registration (`u8_entry.py:161-162`), a caller can make those addresses by registering them, each registration counting one for the account it creates, and then ask for each one's verification four more times, so a drain then needs no real address at all. Step 104(c) records it.
- **Account mail's answer time** (L1-69, with your answers of 2026-11-08, L1-70 to L1-73).
  - Today a signed-out request for a mailed address waits for Resend's synchronous send (`backend/modules/accounts/integrations/account_mail.py:225`, up to 30 s when the tries run out), while an unknown address is answered at once. So the answer's time can tell whether an address has an account and, by which request was slow, its state, which U2's BR2.1 (intent 261010, `u2-account-personal-controls/functional-design/rules.md:104-113`) and SD2-01 (`u2-account-personal-controls/nfr-design/security-design.md:21`) rule out.
  - By your answer, "Send from an outbox", registration and the reset, verification and reactivation requests store their message with its proof and answer at once, the same for every address, and the account-mail sender in the host sends it afterwards with reliability-design § 10's tries (Step 53(h)). A message it cannot deliver yet stays in the outbox under its message key until its proof expires, and a restart resumes it. A slow Resend then delays the mail, never the answer, and no longer holds a host worker thread for each mailed request (the routes run the entry on one, `backend/modules/accounts/local_http.py:140-147`). Step 85(i) shows this through the order of events: every answer arrives while no send has completed.
  - By your answer of 2026-11-08, L1-72 ("Accept as recorded"), the difference that remains is accepted, and no test of this stage or of a later one measures it: an eligible request still makes a few more database writes than an unknown address's (its proof or challenge, its row and, under L1-71, its day's count), the imperfect constant time that SD2-01 does not promise. Step 104(b) records this reading of SD2-01's "Test timing distributions".
  - The signed-in email change and the first sign-in's forced reset keep their synchronous send. The email change mails whatever new address it is given, so its time says nothing about that address, and the forced reset's answer already names the account's reset-required state and its delivery word, by design (BR8.6; `backend/modules/accounts/integrations/account_mail.py:4-5`, `backend/modules/accounts/services/first_sign_in.py:275-284`). By your answer of 2026-11-08, L1-71 ("Check first and cap daily"), the forced reset reads the hold and the allowance's limit first: whenever email is held, Resend is unconfigured or shown as down, or the limit is reached, it says at once that the reset email could not be sent, without calling Resend, and every kind of account email stops at five per account a UTC day (Step 53(i)).
  - One consequence: near the daily limit, a message the request's check admitted may find no place left when the sender delivers it, and then ends unsent. Because a waiting message holds no place until the sender delivers it, near the limit every request admitted while earlier messages wait can end unsent, not only one caught between its check and its send. Its request has already been acknowledged, like every other.
  - Added with this answer, beyond the option, each of which you can turn down at Plan Approval: a stopped sender shows on 운영. Its beat more than 90 s old makes background.work degraded `lane-behind-deadline` ('작업 처리 지연'), and that opens an incident, at the latest past 600 s, and holds the switch's opening gate (Step 53(h)); and a message the sender could not send yet (an unknown outcome, three 429s, or the rehearsal bound) is tried again at most once a minute under the same key until its proof ends, instead of the one delivery that § 10's row reads. By your answer of 2026-11-08, L1-73 ("End refusals after one try"), any other refusal Resend gives, such as a 401, 403 or 422, ends after its one delivery, as that row reads.
  - By your answer of 2026-11-08, L1-70 ("Count on background work"), each delivery or pass of the sender that fails inside the app adds one failed run to background.work's error rate on 운영, beside the lanes' failed jobs, and ordinary sends add nothing. 운영's '작업 실패(24시간)' summary still lists the six lanes only, and no line on 운영 names the sender: with no job ended in the 24 hours, one failed run reads '오류율 100% (측정값)' while every lane reads '실패 0건 / 종료 0건'. The host's log names the sender (`mail.failed`, `mail.pass-failed`). The figure alone opens no incident, but while such failures are in its 24 hours, a degraded, unknown or stale background.work opens its incident at once (Steps 53(h), 58(f)). Resend's refusals already show on provider.resend's figure, an outage on its state and the allowance on 운영's email line. Only these end quietly, all by design: the rehearsal bound's holds; requests stopped at the per-account limit (L1-71), which store no message and leave no figure, summary line or log line that names them; and rows the sender ends before their send because their proof ended or their account changed (Step 53(h), steps 1 and 3).

  - One function, `assistance.job_touch()`, serves two row triggers. Like research's, it has `SET search_path=pg_catalog`, `REVOKE ALL … FROM PUBLIC` and `GRANT EXECUTE … TO docsuri_assistance`.
  - `job_created BEFORE INSERT` sets `NEW.updated_at := NEW.accepted_at`. A column default cannot do this: `accepted_at` defaults to `clock_timestamp()` (`backend/modules/summarization/local_schema.sql:14`), and a second `clock_timestamp()` default would give a slightly different time.
  - `job_touch BEFORE UPDATE` sets `greatest(clock_timestamp(), OLD.updated_at)` when `state` or `failure_code` changes, and keeps `OLD.updated_at` otherwise. So lease bookkeeping, a `phase` change or a direct `SET updated_at` never moves it.

  How it fits with what is built:
  - Row triggers of one kind fire in name order. U1's `bound_execution_deadline` (`BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE`, `local_execution_deadline.sql:12`) fires first and reads no `updated_at`. `job_created` and `job_touch` follow. U1's `preserve_job_binding` (`local_schema.sql:45-63`) fires last and does not read the column.
  - PaperAssistance's insert (`guarded_repository.py:180-182`, written in U1's build) and its `SELECT *` readers stay as built.

### Step 51 — Business logic: CompleteTransactions, per-process counts, the connection table and the job lines — implement

- [x] (a) `backend/u8_counts.py` (new), the processes' failure counts (L1-29):
  - `ProcessCounts(folder, process, *, policy, clock)` belongs to one v2 process (`host`, `workers` or `scheduler`) and writes in the profile's `evidence/` folder. It touches no file until its first append. `record(kind, *, failed)` adds one run to a registered kind's total, and to its failed count when `failed`, in the window open at the clock's now. An unregistered kind raises `ValueError`. A window is `policy.latency_window_seconds` long (300 s in production, 5 s under `SYNTHETIC_OPERATIONS`), aligned to the epoch. The registered kinds are `postgresql.connection` and `postgresql.transaction`. Step 53(h) registers the account-mail sender's kind (L1-70), and Step 56 the providers' kinds.
  - The first `record` after a window ends, and `close()`, append that window's lines: one line for each kind counted in it, `{"failed": n, "kind": k, "total": m, "window": "<window start, UTC, ISO 8601 to the second, Z>"}`, with sorted keys and no identifier or path. One `threading.Lock` covers `record`, the append and `close()`, as `LatencyRecorder` holds its lock (`request_context.py:113-145`), so threads that cross a window end together append it once.
  - Each append opens the folder with `O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW`, making it 0700 when absent, so a folder that is a link is refused at that append. It opens `<process>-counts-<UTC date of the window's start>.jsonl` through the folder's descriptor with `O_RDWR | O_APPEND | O_CREAT | O_NOFOLLOW` at mode 0600. When the file's last byte is not a newline (a write a crash cut short), the lines are preceded by one, so the cut line stays on its own. The lines go out in one `os.write`, then the file is synced.
  - Each append also removes this process's own day files whose day ended at least `policy.latency_retention_seconds` before now (the latency summaries' 14 days). It removes regular files only and never follows a link. A failed append or removal is logged with its error's type (`counts.unwritten`) and never fails a run. A window that could not be written is kept and written with the next append. After `close()`, `record` does nothing.
  - `counts_over(folder, kinds, now)` gives each kind's `(failed, total)`, summed over every process's lines whose window started in the 24 hours before `now`. It reads only the two UTC days that can hold them. Step 58 reads it for storage.capacity.
    - A line that does not parse as JSON (a cut line) is skipped, and a read that skipped any logs one `counts.line-unread` line. One cut line therefore never stops storage.capacity's read for two days.
    - A parsed line outside the shape (its four keys, a registered kind, the window's form, integers with 0 ≤ failed ≤ total) raises `ValueError`. The producer whose count read raised then logs one `counts.unread` line and carries 0 of 0, with its outcome unchanged (Steps 56(d), 58(g) and 58(i)). So one damaged line never makes storage.capacity or a provider unknown.
- [x] (b) `backend/u8_transactions.py` (new): `CompleteTransactions(OwnerTransactions)`, built as `CompleteTransactions(profile, *, process='api', counts=None)`. Before `OwnerTransactions.__init__` reads anything, it refuses a profile that is not a complete realm (`complete_realm`) with its own `ValueError('not a complete realm')`. `OwnerTransactions` and its `run` in `backend/transactions.py` stay as built, so no earlier realm changes.
  - `run(owner, action)` hands `OwnerTransactions.run` the action wrapped. When `CURRENT_REQUEST_ID` (`backend/local_browser.py`) holds a UUID, the wrapper first runs `SELECT set_config('docsuri.request_id', %s, true)` through the bounded connection. The value lasts only for that transaction, every retried attempt sets it again, and Step 47's column defaults read it inside the accept's own transaction (L1-6). A value in any other form is never set, so the defaults' `::uuid` cast cannot fail.
  - Each run is counted once, by the exception that leaves `run` (L1-29):
    - **Failed connection:** `Busy('process connection allocation exhausted')`, `Busy('owner connection allocation exhausted')`, `psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout`, or a `psycopg.OperationalError` or `InterfaceError` raised before the wrapped action began (a refused or failed connect, "too many connections for role").
    - **Failed transaction:** a `psycopg.OperationalError` or `InterfaceError` raised after the action began (`QueryCanceled`, a serialization failure or deadlock re-raised after its three attempts, a lost connection), `UnknownCommit`, `Busy('aggregate transaction deadline reached')` or `Busy('transaction retry budget exhausted')`.
    - **Not counted:** everything else. That includes the action's own errors, `Busy` subclasses (`EntryLimited`, `IdentityStartLimited`, Step 53's `AccountMailLimitReached`) and a plain `Busy` with any other message (`'local account allocation exhausted'`, `'control work deadline reached'`).
  - Every run adds one to `postgresql.connection`'s total. Every run that is not a failed connection adds one to `postgresql.transaction`'s total. With `counts=None` nothing is counted. `close()` closes the counts, then the pools. A run after `close()` records nothing and raises only `OwnerTransactions`' `ValueError('closed or unknown owner pool')`.
  - `u8_host.connect_database(profile, role, *, policy, clock, sleep, on_wait)` now takes the role (`host`, `workers` or `scheduler`) instead of the gate name. It returns `CompleteTransactions(profile, process=PROCESS_GATES[role], counts=ProcessCounts(profile.root / "evidence", role, policy=policy, clock=clock))`, and `compose` passes its role, policy and clock (`u8_host.py:838-840`).

### Step 56 — Business logic: provider probes and failure counts at the composition seams — implement

- [x] (a) **The probes (L1-11, "Active free checks").** New `backend/u8_provider_probes.py`. `worker_producers` (`backend/u8_host.py:1562-1620`) asks it for probes only when `profile.is_production`. A synthetic profile keeps the adapters' passive `reachable()` and the ledger (`producers.py:420-433`), so neither the served realm nor any realm composition in pytest probes.
  - **The request.** Each observation of a configured provider makes one request that carries no credential:
    - Google `GET https://accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration` and ORCID `GET https://orcid.org/.well-known/openid-configuration` pass on a 200;
    - Resend `GET https://api.resend.com/emails` and Notion `GET https://api.notion.com/v1/users/me` pass on any status below 500, 401 included. Neither sends an `Authorization` header. Notion's goes through U6's `GuardedTransport`, which keeps its origin and path pins (`notion_session.py:188-221`), with U6's response cap and a 5.0 s request timeout.

    That is about 1,150 requests a day, at no cost.
  - **The factory.** Each probe takes its base factory as an argument: a client factory for Google, ORCID and Resend, a transport factory for Notion. Production hands each probe its adapter's one guarded network builder, the unwrapped base that item (c) wraps for the adapter's counted calls, looked up as a module attribute at call time: `identity_providers.network_client`, `digest_email.network_client` and `notion_session.network_transport` (`identity_providers.py:49-56`, `digest_email.py:146-149`, `notion_session.py:162-168`), as `OllamaTags` reads `model_runtime.network_transport` (`producers.py:477-487`). So the four checks reach the network only through those builders, no probe is ever counted, the test-wide guard refuses every production probe (`NetworkRefused`, `conftest.py:46-63`), and a test hands in a factory over its own `httpx.MockTransport`. No fifth network builder is added, and none of the adapters' TLS, proxy or retry settings is copied into U8 code. This is L1-11 as you chose it ("Test and synthetic realms never call out. Only U8 files change."), settled on 2026-11-02: the wiring amends no approved text and needs no correction.
  - **The deadline.** There is one whole-probe deadline, `PROBE_SECONDS = 5.0`. It is the same in every profile, because only production probes. The runner:
    - builds the probe's client or transport from its base factory on the calling thread, so a factory that raises fails the probe before any wait;
    - runs the request on a daemon thread (an async request in its own event loop there), which sets a `done` event when the request ends;
    - calls an injected waiter, `waiter(done, POLL_SECONDS)`, while `done` is unset and an injected monotonic clock has moved less than 5.0 s from the start;
    - counts an answer it finds once the clock has moved 5.0 s or more as no answer.

    Production passes `time.monotonic` and `lambda done, step: done.wait(step)` with `POLL_SECONDS = 0.1`, so a fast answer returns at once. The request also carries httpx's own 5.0 s timeout, so an abandoned call ends by itself. Under the test-wide guard every production probe therefore fails with no wait, in the production-profile tests that run every producer too (`test_production_composition.py:95-100`).
  - **A failed probe** makes `ProviderProducer` record unavailable `provider-unreachable` at once. A probe fails on:
    - no answer within 5.0 s;
    - a transport error, a guard refusal or `NetworkRefused`;
    - a 5xx;
    - a discovery document that does not answer 200.

    This amends reliability-design § 10's probe row ("its last state ages into stale"); the amendment is recorded as a correction in the code summary.
  - **Probe and passive check together.** `ProviderProducer` gains `probe`, an optional keyword, which it checks first. The adapter's passive `reachable()` stays the second input, but only within one process: sign-in exchanges and account mail run in the host (`u8_entry.py:254-258`, `first_sign_in.py:275`), while `ProviderProducer` reads the workers' own adapters (`provider_reachability`, `u8_host.py:1651-1666`), whose flags never turn False. So in production the probe alone turns Google, ORCID and Resend unavailable. Step 56 does not change `account_mail.py`; Step 53(g)'s up-front check reads the `provider.resend` state this producer records.

- [x] (b) **The model runtime's bounds.** In `OllamaTags` (`producers.py:470-498`):
  - `tags()` runs under its own `PROBE_SECONDS`;
  - `repin()` runs under its own `REPIN_SECONDS = 10.0`, which covers the search model's measured first load of 1.7 to 4.9 s (performance-design § 2.6).

  Each runs through item (a)'s runner, with an httpx timeout of the same length, and the one shared `timeout=10.0` is removed. The clock and the waiter are optional keywords, defaulting to production's. `ModelsProducer` calls both as built, so a call past its deadline reads unavailable `runtime-unreachable` at once (`producers.py:450-453, :462-466`).

- [x] (c) **The counting layers (L1-12, "At the U8 seams").** `backend/u8_provider_probes.py` holds two wrappers:
  - a client-factory wrapper, which adds one response hook to each client its base factory builds;
  - a transport-factory wrapper, which returns a new delegating transport over `base()` on every call.

  The counting rule:
  - an answered 4xx other than 429 is a refusal, and a 429 is over the limit; both count as errors;
  - every answered call adds 1 to the total;
  - a transport error, a guard refusal or `NetworkRefused` adds to neither;
  - a sign-in the person cancels never reaches the provider, so it is never counted.

  Each wrapper adds to its process's u8_counts writer (Step 51(a)). `backend/u8_counts.py` registers the kinds `provider.google`, `provider.orcid`, `provider.resend` and `provider.notion`. The wrappers are wired at U8's seams, in production only, and no earlier unit's file changes:

Its `_network_client` becomes the public `network_client`. `build_account_controls` (`u8_host.py:464-470`) passes the wrapper over it.
  - **Account mail.** `_wire_production` (`u8_host.py:959-962`) passes `ResendAccountMail` the wrapper over `digest_email.network_client`, through the adapter's existing `client_factory`.
  - **Digests.** `u8_outward.digest_mail` (`u8_outward.py:256-274`) gains a `client_factory` keyword and passes `GatedResendDigestMail` the same wrapper. The adapter already takes that argument (`u8_digest_mail.py:66-73`), so `u8_digest_mail.py` does not change.
  - **Notion.** `u8_outward.production_export` (`u8_outward.py:391-397`) passes U6's export contribution the transport-factory wrapper over `notion_session.network_transport`, instead of `transport_factory=None`.
    - `NotionSession` calls its factory once per operation and wraps the result in `GuardedTransport` (`notion_session.py:458-462, :533-542`). So every operation keeps its own counted transport and its own SDK client (NFR3.1).
    - Under the real policy, `u6_host.bound_transport` accepts the factory the way it accepts its documented test seam (`u6_host.py:73-85`).
    - U6's files stay as built. Production's use of that seam is recorded as a correction in the code summary.

  `identity_providers.py`, the one accounts file this step changes, imports nothing from ServiceOperations (`PORT_OWNERS`, `u8_registry.py:458-461`): `u8_host.py` hands the wrapper in.

- [x] (d) **Counts on every outcome.** `ProviderProducer` takes a count reader, an optional keyword, and carries `error_count` and `total_count` on each of its outcomes: a failed probe, unreachable, held, an unavailable activation, allowance exhausted and available (`producers.py:420-433`). It reads the counts only after its outcome is settled: a count read that raises is logged once (`operations`, `counts.unread`, `state` the capability) and counts 0 of 0, so a count never changes an outcome. In every profile, `worker_producers` passes u8_counts' 24-hour reader of every process's count files (host, workers and scheduler) for the producer's kind. In the realm nothing writes those files, so the counts read 0 of 0. Without a reader the counts read 0 of 0 and every outcome is as built (`test_producers.py:41-61, :308-321`).

### Step 58 — Business logic: observations, producers' error counts and the scheduler pass — implement

- [x] (a) **The observation buffer (NFR9.2; L1-46).** `Observations.record` (`observations.py:117-133`) writes what is buffered and the new rows together, oldest first, in inserts of at most 60 rows (`MAX_INSERT`, `observation_store.py:30, :83-86`).
  - A refused insert stops the writing. Only then, while more than 60 rows remain, does it drop the oldest and count them. So a row is dropped only while the store refuses and the buffer is full. Today `ProducerBuffer.add` drops before the write is even tried (`observations.py:64-68, :119-121`).
  - Every row it writes carries the producer's running dropped count as Step 49's `dropped_count`. The buffer keeps the rows it could not write unchanged.
  - Under L1-46, the count lasts as long as the producing process, and is 0 again after a workers restart.
  - `CapabilityState` (`readiness.py:40-52`) gains `dropped_count`. `Readiness._one` reads it from the latest row as `row.get("dropped_count", 0)`, because the rows of `test_readiness.py:22-26` carry no such field.
- [x] (b) **platform.status (NFR9.7's backup-agent row).** `PlatformStatusProducer` (`producers.py:329-343`) also takes, as optional keywords, the agent's status reader (`agent_status_reader`, `u8_host.py:1637-1648`), the ledger, the environment and the policy. Its outcomes:
  - with no inspect reader, or inspect answering anything but pass, available or degraded: unknown `evidence-unavailable`, as built;
  - with no agent reader bound: inspect's outcome alone, as built (`test_producers.py:265-267`);
  - with an agent status that has findings: degraded, the first finding as the reason and every finding as a limitation, whether inspect passed or was degraded;
  - with a healthy agent status: available when inspect passed; degraded `evidence-unavailable` when inspect was degraded, as built;
  - with no status recorded (`EvidenceStatus` raises `LookupError`, `backup_agent/status.py:219-225`): unknown `evidence-unavailable` when inspect passed, never `producer-failed`; degraded `evidence-unavailable` when inspect was degraded.

  **The counts.** Every outcome carries `error_count` and `total_count` over the policy's 24 hours, read under item (i)'s rule. They come from the ledger's records of the agent's work in this environment, and never through `receipt_reader`.
  - **Writes.** Each backup write counts once, and fails when its request failed or its unowned set's integrity failed:
    - a `backup.create` request settled `succeeded` or `failed`, of any origin, at its `updatedAt`; its own set is part of it;
    - a set whose `recoveryRequestId` names no `backup.create` request (`first-live`, `pre-release`, pre- and post-restore sets), at its `takenAt`.

    A ledger copy with a `backupId` is part of its set's write, because a copy that fails fails its set (`ledger-copy-failed`, `recovery_procedures.py:262-272`). A copy taken on its own (L1-5) counts as one write, at its `takenAt`, and it fails when it was recorded without `verifiedAt` because its chain check failed (Step 64(c) records it that way, after its `storage.capacity` signal). Like the failed `first-live`, `pre-release`, pre- and post-restore writes below, it is not counted, and Step 104(c)'s record of this limit names it with them. A write that failed before any set was recorded (the agent's effect itself failed, `recovery_procedures.py:236-239`) is counted only through its `backup.create` request. A failed `first-live`, `pre-release`, pre- or post-restore write leaves no set and no such request, so it is not counted: the count covers the failures the ledger holds, and this limit is recorded in the code summary.

A ledger copy without a set, and every retained copy, has no environment field (`ledger_records.py:447-504`) and belongs to this machine rather than to one database, so it counts in the environment the producer serves (`composition.environment`): during the soak, rehearsal.

### Step 60 — Business logic: the operations dashboard's contents — implement

- [x] (a) **The month's figure (L1-45).** `Dashboard` (`dashboard.py:164-169`) takes the operations policy, an optional keyword that defaults to `PRODUCTION_OPERATIONS`. It builds its `AvailabilityRecord` with the policy's `availability_slot_seconds`. Today `dashboard.py:310` uses the 300 s default, while the realm's heartbeat writes 5 s slots (`u8_policy.py:273`, `standing/main.py:294-295`).
  - A new `u8_host.operations_dashboard(composition, operations)` builds the host's dashboard, and `_operations_router` (`u8_host.py:1352-1369`) calls it. It passes `composition.policy`, the folder from `availability_folder(composition)` (Step 58(e)), and the inputs of items (d) and (e).
  - `_availability` reads `cutover-record` through `ledger.records`, without `_records`' environment filter, because the record has no `environment` field (`ledger_records.py:550-580`). It passes the newest record's `admissionOpenedAt` to `figure()` as `opened_at`; today `dashboard.py:315` passes none.
  - Under L1-45, as built: a month with no line has no item (`dashboard.py:313-314`), and before admission opens, the month counts from its start.
- [x] (b) **The standing job (NFR9.7's standing-job row; L1-41).** One `operations.standing-job` item:
  - `observedAt` is the newest line's `slot`, across the current and the previous Seoul month files. A down line counts too, because the heartbeat writes a line for every slot it runs (`standing/heartbeat.py:84-89`). `ageSeconds` is `now` minus that slot.
  - It is late while `ageSeconds` is above two of the policy's slots (600 s in production: healthchecks.io's period plus grace, observability-design § 5), and then carries the limitation `standing-job-late`. Its status is degraded while it is late or while any failure count below is above 0, and available otherwise.
  - When neither file has a line, it is unknown with `standing-job-unrecorded`, `observedAt` `now` and no age. A month file the dashboard cannot read gives it unknown with `availability-record-unreadable`, as `_availability` does (`dashboard.py:316-320`).

  Its limitations count the standing job's own runs, requests with origin `schedule`, over the policy's 24 hours, in this environment, each request once at its `updatedAt`:
  - `failed-backups:<n>`: `backup.create` requests that ended `failed`, `refused` or `expired`. A request's own failed-integrity set is counted with it.
  - `failed-verifications:<n>`: `restore.verify` requests that ended `failed`, `refused` (such as `refused:internal-disk-low`, `recovery.py:403-407`) or `expired`. A request's own failed verification record (`verificationId` is `uuid5` of `docsuri-verification:<request id>`, `recovery_procedures.py:380`) is counted with it.
  - `failed-disposals:<n>`: undisposed sets, ledger copies and retained copies whose `lastDisposalFailedAt` (Step 58(h)) is in the window, so a disposal still failing after a day counts at its latest attempt. A rehearsal database still in use never carries that field, so it is never a failure, and a waiting rehearsal set is left out as Step 58(b) leaves it out. Ledger copies and retained copies count in the environment Step 58(b) gives them: for one with none, the environment this dashboard serves.

  `ScheduledRecovery` pings `/fail` for each of these runs (`standing/main.py:139-141, :168-174`). Administrator requests, and sets no request owns (`first-live`, `pre-release`, pre- and post-restore), are the operator's work: they count in platform.status's writes (Step 58(b)), never here. A cancelled request ran nothing. A run that left no request (the verification lane with no passed set, `standing/main.py:158-161`) leaves nothing in the ledger; healthchecks.io still reports it.
- [x] (c) **The latency panel's error rate.** `_latency` (`dashboard.py:278-303`) adds `error-rate-permille:<errors5xx * 1000 // count>` to each class whose newest window has a count above 0, and nothing to an idle class. The panel's rate covers the newest window; public.static's capability rate covers Step 58(c)'s 24 hours.
- [x] (d) **Verifications and stop records.**
  - `RESTORE_VERIFICATION` (`ledger_records.py:416-433`) registers two optional counts: `hnswRebuildSeconds`, and its projection to the 8 GiB budget, `hnswProjectedSeconds` (scalability-design § 5, the HNSW row of the growth signals). The projection scales the measured time linearly by the restored set's size and is rounded up to whole seconds, as Step 62(d) rounds the time itself: `hnswProjectedSeconds = ceil(hnswRebuildSeconds × footprint_budget_bytes / sourceDatabaseBytes)`, computed in integers as `(hnswRebuildSeconds * footprint_budget_bytes + sourceDatabaseBytes - 1) // sourceDatabaseBytes`, with the policy's `footprint_budget_bytes` (8 GiB in both policies, `u8_policy.py:106`). A set whose `sourceDatabaseBytes` is 0 (`_record_set` records 0 when the agent's facts carry no `databaseBytes`, `recovery_procedures.py:290`) gets `hnswRebuildSeconds` and no projection, so nothing divides by zero. Step 62(d) measures the time, and Step 64(i) records both. They amend RestoreVerification's attribute list in entities.md (`:750-812`); the amendment is recorded as a correction in the code summary.
  - `_verifications` (`dashboard.py:232-247`) adds `restore-bound-seconds:<the policy's restore_recreate_and_restore_seconds>` to every verification item; that is 2,700 in production (`u8_policy.py:96`). It adds `hnsw-rebuild-seconds:<n>` whenever the record has `hnswRebuildSeconds`, and `hnsw-projected-seconds:<n>` only when it has `hnswProjectedSeconds`, with `hnsw-projection-past-bound` when that projection is above the bound. A set of 0 bytes therefore shows its rebuild time with no projection, and is never past the bound.
  - `Dashboard` takes the isolation folder, which `operations_dashboard` gives as `producers.isolation_folder(profile, composition.arrangement)` (`producers.py:590-600`). It adds one `operations.isolation-result` item from the newest result file, picked as `IsolationProducer` picks it (`producers.py:355-364`):
    - `observedAt` is the file's `checkedAt`, and the evidence is `isolation:<resultId>`;
    - it carries one limitation, `stop:<label>:<expiresAt>`, per stop record (`label`, `receiptId`, `stoppedAt`, `expiresAt`, `u8_platform/fixed.py:198-199`), and none when the file has none;
    - with no result file, there is no item. A newest file that cannot be read or parsed, or lacks `checkedAt`, `resultId` or `stopRecords`, gives one unknown item with `isolation-result-unreadable`, and every other item still shows.
  - Every set item stays (`dashboard.py:204-230`), because the restore chooser needs them. Showing each database's newest set is the view's job (L1-52, Step 93(c)).
- [x] (e) **Failed jobs per lane (L1-41).** `Dashboard` takes a lane-count reader. `operations_dashboard` passes Step 58(f)'s `LaneCounts` over the host's own owner logins:
  - each lane is one short transaction;
  - the export lane goes through `export.status_counts`, never a read of export's tables;
  - it adds no connection to L1-13's table, which already counts the host's owner logins.

  There is one `operations.lane` item per lane, with the lane as its component: `research`, `assistance`, `topics`, `export`, `corpus` and `lifecycle`. Each carries `failed:<n>` and `terminal:<n>`. Its status is degraded when `failed` is above 0 and available otherwise, the same rule the latency items apply to their 5xx count (`dashboard.py:297`). A lane answered None (its read failed) gives its item unknown with `lane-count-unavailable` and no counts, and the other lanes still show: one failing source never fails the whole read, which `answer()` would turn into a 500 (`http.py:113-124`). The module docstring lists the new items.
- [x] (f) **Missing observations (NFR9.2).** `_capabilities` (`dashboard.py:181-198`) adds `missing-observations:<n>` to a capability whose state's `dropped_count` (Step 58(a)) is above 0.

A set has kind `backup-set` and its `retainUntil`; a staging file a write left behind has kind `staging-file` and `takenAt + 86,400 s`; a retained copy has its own kind and its date with (e)'s tails; a volume file below has kind `volume-file` and its catalogue date.
    - `retired`: one `{volume, retiredAt, count}` per retired volume, as BR2.5 (rules.md:136) lists a copy retired with a lost volume "as retired with that encrypted volume on that date". `volume` is the retirement decision's `subjectRef`, found through the closing version's `retirementReceiptRef` ((h)); a record retired without one is grouped with `volume` null. A list per record would grow by some 45 records at each retirement and, past the bound below, would hold every later erasure for good.
  - The volume files come from the agent's latest status: the `backup-volume` evidence the standing job records (Step 66(f)), read in full (`observations`, `observedAt`, `maxAgeSeconds`) through the platform part's evidence reader. `EvidenceStatus` (`status.py:219-226`) returns the observations alone, so it is not used here.
    - A status is usable when it was observed within its `maxAgeSeconds`, its `catalogue` is `intact`, its `deletionAllowed` is true (no finding but low free space: a volume of another identity would list another volume's files) and it carries `unrecordedCount`.
    - Each entry of a usable status's `unrecordedFiles` whose `recordId` the ledger still has no BackupSet, LedgerCopy or RetainedCopy for is counted in `unrecordedCounted` and dated by its `disposeAfter`. An entry without a date holds the scope (`volume-file-undated`). So does an `unrecordedCount` above the listed entries (`volume-files-over-bound`).
    - In production, where the standing job records a status every 5 minutes, the scope holds without a usable one: `agent-status-stale` when the latest is older than its `maxAgeSeconds`, else `agent-status-unrecorded`. BR2.5 names every file the ledger has no record of, and a missing or old status there is a fault.
    - In a realm, which need run no standing job (the served realm runs none), the evidence then names no volume file and records `agentStatusRecorded: false`. A usable status records `agentStatusRecorded: true`.
    - A reader that raises `ControlError` (the store unreachable, or the reader login at its connection limit) holds the scope with `platform-reader-unavailable`.
  - `_evidence` for `restore_enforcement` (`:178-196`) adds the covering verification's `verificationStartedAt` and `verificationFinishedAt`. It also adds `verificationStartLate: true` when the start falls more than `erasure_verification_start_seconds` (86,400 s) after the tombstone's `appendedAt` (L1-42).
  - `LIFECYCLE_EVIDENCE` (`ledger_records.py:762-776`) refuses unregistered fields (`:206-213`). It now registers `undisposed` and `retired` (at most 256 items each, which keeps the record within the ledger's 64 KiB entry bound, `ledger.py:48`; more holds the scope with `backups-evidence-over-bound`), `unrecordedCounted`, `agentStatusRecorded`, `verificationStartedAt`, `verificationFinishedAt` and `verificationStartLate`.

### Step 66 — Business logic: the standing job — implement

- [x] (a) **A waiting erasure is verified at the next 05:00 (L1-42).**
  - `weekly_at` (`lanes.py:64-78`) passes its 05:00 candidate to `also`, not `now`.
  - `ScheduledRecovery.erasure_waits(at)` (`main.py:183-187`, which ignores its instant today) holds only for an uncovered `restore-tombstone` appended at or before `at`.
  - `verification_due(now)` (`:189-197`) is due in two cases: no verification of the environment started at or after the latest Sunday 05:00; or an erasure waited at the latest 05:00 and none has started since. So a restart catches up only an erasure that a missed 05:00 left waiting (R4).
  - A tombstone appended after a day's 05:00 is verified at the next day's 05:00, within 24 hours.
- [x] (b) **A day without a passed set still gets its ledger copy (NFR4.3, NFR9.6, L1-5, L1-48).**
  - Before it files anything, the 04:00 turn settles what an interrupted turn left open, after `settle_unknown` (`main.py:106-128`):
    - `procedures.reconcile_interrupted(("ledger-copy", "database-production", "database-rehearsal"))` (Step 64(j)) settles the scheduler's own operations on those targets that a stopped process left pending past their lease or unresolved. No request carries a lone copy, so `settle_unknown` never sees it, and the store refuses any other actor (`u8_store.sql:116-127`). A store that refuses is caught, and the turn goes on.
    - A scheduled `backup.create` of either environment that an earlier day's turn left `running` (its process stopped mid-effect) is run again through `procedures.backup`, which takes the request's own environment. Its bound operation's key is unchanged (`_key` reads the request's revision, which nothing moved since its start, `recovery_procedures.py:148-150`), so the receipt replays and the request settles, as a retry the same day does. Left `running`, it would hold every later request (`conflicting-request-active`) and every backups scope (Step 64(g)).
    - `settle_unknown` (`main.py:106-128`) likewise reads the scheduled `unknown` requests of both environments, through `requests.unknown()` with no environment (`recovery.py:119-120`), where today it reads the current one only (`main.py:119`). A switch, an abort or a rollback changes the mode between two turns, Step 64(g)'s wait reads a request of either environment, and only the standing job can settle its own operations (`recovery_procedures.py:704-716`), so a request the earlier mode left would otherwise hold every backups scope for good.
  - `platform.database_of(environment)` raising `no-rehearsal-database` (`main.py:134`; rehearsal mode before the first accepted dry run, `recovery_procedures.py:109-115`) is caught: no request is filed, the lone copy below is taken, and the turn answers `no-rehearsal-database`.
  - A 04:00 turn that ends without a passed set calls `procedures.ledger_copy_alone(environment, owner_key="standing-ledger-copy:<environment>:<YYYYMMDD>", via="standing")`. The date is the Seoul date of that 04:00 instant, and the copy runs through `execute_settled` (Step 64(c)): a retry the same day returns an applied copy and runs a failed one again under the next retry key.
  - Such a turn is one where there is no rehearsal database, the backup was not admitted, the set was refused or failed, its integrity failed, its copy failed, or its outcome is unknown.
  - The lane then pings `/backup/fail` once, whatever the copy's outcome. The copy is admitted while a switch or a production restore holds the environment (L1-48).
  - A copy that does not complete (`ledger_copy_alone` raises `ProcedureFailed`, or `OutcomeUnknown` while its outcome is still unknown) has already signalled `storage.capacity` (Step 64(c)). The turn catches either and answers `ledger-copy-failed` in place of the backup's key; it still pings `/backup/fail` once, and still runs the disposal pass below when it ran `procedures.backup`. A failed backup keeps its request's `failed:<reason>` and its own incident, and a backup not admitted keeps its `requested` request until it expires (NFR7.10); 운영 counts those requests (Step 60(b)), so the turn's key reaches only the standing job's `lane.ran` log line (`main.py:341-343`). Otherwise the turn's result keys stay `backup-not-admitted`, `backup-failed` and `no-rehearsal-database`. A passed set takes no extra copy.
  - The disposal pass runs after every turn that ran `procedures.backup`, whether the set passed or not, after the ping:
    - tech-stack-decisions.md:70 and BR9.17 (rules.md:892) run it "after each scheduled backup", and reliability-design § 6 step 4 follows the set with it. Today a failed backup runs none (`main.py:143-147`).
    - With low free space the only finding, the agent refuses the backup but still deletes (`status.py:182-185`), and `AgentStatus` never runs the pass, because `available` stays false (`main.py:65-77`). Without this, expired sets would never go and backups would never resume.
    - The pass still refuses while an exclusion holds (`cutover/disposal.py:140-143`). A day whose backup was not admitted runs none.
- [x] (c) **A failing lane never stops the job (logical-components § 2).**
  - `FAILING_ON_SKIP` becomes `CHECKED_LANES` (`lanes.py:33`). No test imports the name.
  - `_launch`'s `except` branch (`:161-164`) records `lane-failed` and then calls `self.fail(lane.name)` for a checked lane.
  - `start` (`:125-135`) and `tick` (`:137-153`) catch an exception from a lane's `catch_up` or `latest`, one lane at a time, and go on with the other lanes:
    - The lane records one failed turn (`lane-failed`), and a checked lane pings `/fail` once, per scheduled turn.
    - A turn is identified by its instant: for the verification lane, whose `latest` reads the ledger, it is that day's 05:00 candidate; for the backup lane, that day's 04:00.
  - A lane whose `catch_up` raised at start asks it again at each tick, and launches nothing, until it answers once; then it runs or waits as at start. So an overdue backup, or a verification a missed 05:00 left due, starts at the first tick the ledger answers (R4, NFR7.7), not a day later.
  - A lane whose `latest` raised at start counts as started at that turn's instant, so it waits for its next scheduled turn. Today `last_started` would stay None, and `tick` skips its due check for None (`:144`), so the lane would launch at the first tick that answers, on a day the lane table may not name.
  - A `latest` that raises at a later tick leaves `last_started` as it was and is asked again at the next tick.
  - A succeeded backup pings ok before its disposal pass (`main.py:144-146`), so a disposal pass that raises pings `/backup/fail` last.
  - The module docstring (`:15-19`) says so.
- [x] (d) **A hard 10 seconds per probe (R1, R4).**
  - `heartbeat.probe` (`heartbeat.py:43-59`) runs the request in a daemon thread and waits for it for at most `seconds`. Its `opener` (default `urllib.request.urlopen`), `clock` (default `time.monotonic`) and `waiter` (default `Thread.join`) are injectable.
  - It answers `Answer("timeout")` when the thread is still alive at the limit, or when the answer came after it. DNS, connect, TLS and a slow answer all fall inside the limit.
  - So the sequential pair (`:86`) ends within 2 × 10 s, under the lane's 25 s bound.
  - Step 58(e)'s `public-timeout` and `local-timeout` keep each timeout attributed (L1-30).
  - `test_availability.py:147-158`'s real-server probe still passes.

  - When it starts, or launchd relaunches it, the standing job starts one start watch, in a daemon thread of its own and not a lane. Every 5 s on its clock, the watch runs the heartbeat's local probe within its 10 s limit (`probe(<local>, seconds=policy.probe_limit_seconds)`), until the probe answers ready (status 200) or 600 s have passed since the start.
  - It then appends one synced line to `<scheduler folder>/evidence/starts/<YYYY-MM-DD>.jsonl`, named by the start's UTC day: `{startedAt, readyAt, seconds}`, or `{startedAt, readyAt: null}` when the bound passed first. It probes nothing after that.

  - The folder is 0700 and the file 0600, opened with `O_APPEND | O_NOFOLLOW` and never through a link. It is never written in the 0755 availability folder. One line is written per process start.
  - Hourly housekeeping (`housekeeping.py:25-41`) gains a part, `prunedStarts`, that deletes this folder's day files more than 14 days old, judged by name. It is a new `Housekeeping` field, declared before `batch` with a default that prunes nothing, so the three-argument constructions (`test_standing_lanes.py:286`, `:300`) stay valid.
  - The watch is a `StandingParts` part with a default of none, after `slot_seconds`. `realm_parts` (`main.py:260-321`) and `production_parts` (`production_wiring.py:496-546`) wire it and the housekeeping part, and `production_main` and the realm entry (`main.py:324-394`) start it before `run_forever`. Production's folder is `/Library/DocSuri/scheduler/evidence/starts/`; the realm's is `<run root>/scheduler/evidence/starts/`.

### Step 68 — Business logic: the migration tool, its disk guard and the synthetic v1's objects — implement

- [x] (a) **The disk guard reads its estimate at every guard (L1-17).** `MigrationTool` (`ops/src/docsuri_ops/migration/tool.py:94-100`) loses `estimate_bytes=0`. No builder passes it (`migration/words.py:452`, `migration/production.py:438`), so today a dry run counts no rehearsal database at all. `_guard(run, snapshot)` (`:274-279`) reads both of its figures again at every call:
  - **Still to write:** the snapshot's `sourceDatabaseBytes` plus the estimate. The estimate is `database_bytes` of the latest accepted dry run's rehearsal database (`MigrationRuns.latest_accepted("dry")`, the latest by `startedAt`) while that run's target copy is open (`target_disposed` is false). Otherwise it is `copies.policy.first_rehearsal_estimate_bytes` (4 GiB, `backend/u8_policy.py:113`, which no code reads today). Rejected, failed and final runs never count.
  - **Already held:** `database_bytes` of the run's target, plus `database_bytes` of its import database once the run's `import-database` copy is recorded. The import database is read from the open copy; `_guard` never records one. BR6.6 subtracts what both databases hold. Today only the target is subtracted (`:276-278`), so the guard after the restore counts the restored dump as still to be written.

  The guards before and after the import restore (`:284`, `:287`) stay where they are, and a refusal is still `Interrupted("internal-disk-low")`. A final run counts the same estimate: the accepted run's rehearsal database, which the profile still names during the switch. L1-17 also corrects two texts. NFR8.14's and § 3.3's "23 GiB" becomes ≈24.2 GiB (the 20 GiB threshold, v1's 0.23 GB dump and the 4 GiB estimate). BR6.6's "v1's dumped size while no dry run is accepted" becomes the 4 GiB estimate. Both corrections go into the code summary with Step 104(b)'s, and the approved texts are never edited.
- [x] (b) **A running import stops at its next boundary (S3).**
  - `ImportRun` (`backend/modules/operations/migration/phases.py:155-170`) takes `boundary`. It is called with `"phase"` before each of `PHASES`, and with `"paper"` at the top of each iteration of `_papers` (`:267`), before the paper is read. By default it does nothing, so every existing caller is unchanged.
  - `DiskGuard` (`migration/disk_guard.py`) gains `critical_bytes` (by default the policy's `internal_disk_critical_bytes`, 10 GiB in both policies), `CRITICAL = "internal-disk-critical"`, `DiskStopped(reason)` and `boundary(*, to_write, held)`. The check that `boundary` returns reads the free space once per call:
    - below the critical floor it raises `DiskStopped(CRITICAL)` at either kind of boundary;
    - at a phase start it also applies the room rule, reading `held()` at that moment (`DiskStopped(LOW)`).

    The docstring's "again before each import phase" is then true.
  - **The realm.** `_import_here` passes `self.platform.disk.boundary(...)` with `_guard`'s figures and turns `DiskStopped` into `Interrupted(reason)`. The run is then interrupted at `importing`, and `resume` runs that phase again. `_verify`'s idempotency pass writes nothing, so it runs without a boundary.
  - **Production.**
    - `_request` adds `toWrite`, the figure `_guard` gives when the request is made. The key joins `IMPORT_HEADER` (`ops/src/docsuri_ops/production_wiring.py:949-950`), and `production_import` requires it for its `import` word.
    - `production_import` gains `free_bytes` (by default `free_space(paths)`, below). For `import` only, it builds the check from `PRODUCTION_OPERATIONS`' threshold and floor. `held` is the sum of `pg_database_size(current_database())` read through the import connection and through the target's owner transactions, so each login measures only its own database.
    - A `DiskStopped` answers `{"interrupted": reason}`.
  - `_import_through_program` (`tool.py:329-341`) reads `interrupted` before anything else. `internal-disk-low` or `internal-disk-critical` raises `Interrupted(reason)`; any other value is `import-answer-refused`. `_import_here` and `_import_through_program` take `to_write` as a keyword.
  - **One production free-space reader.** `production_wiring.free_space(paths)` is `shutil.disk_usage(paths.prefix).free`, which is `f_bavail × f_frsize`. It replaces the lambdas at `production_wiring.py:483`, `production_wiring.py:1265` and `migration/production.py:434`; that `DiskGuard` also passes `policy.internal_disk_critical_bytes`. The realm's guard (`migration/words.py:446`) passes `SYNTHETIC_OPERATIONS.internal_disk_critical_bytes`.

Under L1-3 a date is computed from the event the policy names, and you never type one.
  - **The decide step shows the rule, not a date to type.**

A document carrying `finalSnapshotDisposeAfter`, `v1StoresDisposeAfter` or `rolledBackDisposeAfter` is refused with `word-or-input-refused`. `Kind.dated` and `_dated` go, and the module's table (`decide.py:18-29`) follows.

    - `settle(approval_id, subject)`: on a `switched` record, `Cutover.settle` moves it as today and records `settledAt`, the move's instant. On a `settled` record (a re-date that was cut short), it goes straight to the re-date. In both cases the final snapshot named by the subject's `finalSnapshotCopyId` is re-dated to `settledAt` plus `final_snapshot_disposal_seconds`. The anchor is the move, not your decision: NFR3.12 counts 30 days from the settlement, and the decide step checks only that the record is `switched` (`decide.py:111-114`), so a settlement can be decided days before the window ends.

A missing day file reads as empty, and a malformed line is skipped. A line counts when its `window` starts at or after `start` and ends, `window_seconds` later, at or before `end`. For every class of `ROUTE_CLASSES` it answers the largest window `p95Ms` (null when no counted window holds a request) and the sum of `count`, with the number of distinct windows: the cautious reading that `scripts/u8_phases.py`'s `latency_summaries` takes for NFR8.3.

### Step 72 — Business logic: keys, the production environment tool and the operator tool — implement

- [x] (a) **The search cursor key lives in its own folder (L1-4).**
  - **A U8 reader.** In `backend/u8_host.py`, `cursor_key_path(profile)` is `key_folder(profile, "cursor-key") / "search-cursor.key"`. `read_cursor_key(profile)` reads it with `O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK`. It requires a regular file of this process's user, at mode 0600, with one link and exactly 32 bytes; otherwise, a missing file included, it raises `ValueError`. It never creates the key.
  - **Where it is used.** It replaces U3's `_cursor_key` at U8's three call sites: `build_paper_corpus`'s `CompleteSearch` (`u8_host.py:516-532`), `_research_routers`' `JobListCursor` (`:1341-1344`) and `production_corpus` (`u8_outward.py:171-185`). `backend/u3_host.py` and its root file stay as built for U3's realm.
  - **The start.** After its verifier check, `start_keys` (`u8_host.py:355-372`) refuses with `StartRefused("key-folders", "cursor-key-missing-with-accounts")` when accounts exist and the cursor key is missing, so a start missing both keys names the verifier first. Otherwise it runs `ensure_key_file(cursor_key_path(profile))`, which creates the key only when it is missing, that is, while no account exists. The root's `search-cursor.key` is no longer created.
  - **Creating it while no account exists.** The realm's `migrate` creates the key (Step 47(e)). `host_flows.production_stand_in` writes the key only when it imports an account (`maintainer=True`): `ensure_key_file(cursor_key_path(profile))` runs beside `ensure_verifier_key` (`host_flows.py:409-412`), before it yields, so a stand-in with an account holds both keys, as a started production does. A stand-in without an account holds neither key, and a compose of it creates both through `start_keys(profile, occupied=False)` (Step 88(a)). `research_flows.production_research` builds its parts without `compose`, so it first runs that same `start_keys(standin.profile, occupied=False)`, as a start runs it before any builder. Otherwise `production_corpus`'s `read_cursor_key` would refuse a missing key in `component/test_research_execution.py`, `integration/test_large_paper_assistance.py` and `integration/test_model_lane.py`. `tests/u8_service_operations_integration/research_flows.py` joins this step's files.

    Without these, every compose after a realm's first account would be refused.
  - **The new in-person word `replace-cursor-key`.** It joins `production_tool.py`'s `WORDS`, `CONSEQUENCES` (`open-cursors-restart`) and its dispatch.
    - While any of v2's three roles runs, it is refused with `cursor-key-replace-refused` (detail `v2-running`) and writes nothing, as `control-key-start` is (`context.v2_stopped()`, `production_tool.py:901-918`).
    - With v2 stopped, it writes 32 random bytes to a staging file in `cursor-key/` (0600, `O_EXCL | O_NOFOLLOW`), syncs it, replaces the key with it and syncs the folder. A missing key is created the same way.
    - `render.PRODUCTION_TOOL_WORDS` gains the word in the same place, so it renders in `DOCSURI_INPERSON_SERVICE` only and in no standing set. `templates/sudoers` is unchanged, because its aliases come from `render.py`.
  - **The installation runbook.** `u8-installation-runbook.md:87` names the cursor key beside the verifier key that v2's first start creates.
    - **§ 5** gains `replace-cursor-key`. Unlike the settings words there, it runs only while v2 is stopped:
      1. Stop v2's three roles (`service stop <label>`, three password prompts each, as phase 7's keyring start does).
      2. Run `docsuri-production-tool replace-cursor-key`.
      3. Start the roles again (`service start <label>`).

      Open search and job-list pages then restart at their first page.
    - **"If something goes wrong"** gains the start's `cursor-key-missing-with-accounts`, with that procedure as its way out. A rebuild after this Mac is lost always meets it, since no key is in a backup.
    - **Corrections.** Step 104 records in the code summary that BR4.8's and BR6.2's key-loss rules and reliability-design § 9's rebuild rule gain `replace-cursor-key`.

Migrate's key is Step 47(e)'s, and its test Step 48(h)'s.
- [x] (b) **The operator tool reports the availability figure (NFR9.13).** A new `ops/src/docsuri_ops/u8_platform/availability_words.py` is routed by `operator_tool.py`, whose `COMMANDS` and `USAGE` gain `availability`. Its form is `availability report [--month YYYY-MM] (--production | --environment-file PATH)`.
  - **The record.** It reads the record folder directly, with no sudo and no subprocess. In production that is `ArrangementPaths().availability` (0755, its files 0644) with `PRODUCTION_OPERATIONS.availability_slot_seconds` (300). In the realm it is the run root's `availability/` with `SYNTHETIC_OPERATIONS`' slot (5).
  - **The opening.** It reads the CutoverRecord's `admissionOpenedAt` through the in-person ledger read. In production that is `LedgerClient(via="in-person")`, which uses `sudo -k` and asks for your password. In the realm it is the realm's ledger; when that ledger does not exist yet, there is no opening.
  - **The result.** One JSON result, with `month`, `closed` (true for a month before the current Seoul month) and `admissionOpenedAt` (null when there is no opening):
    - for the opening's month and every later month, `AvailabilityRecord.figure(month, now, opened_at=…)` as `Figure.as_dict()`. For the current month that is the running figure and the budget left; for `--month` it is that closed month's figure over all its slots, counted from the opening in the opening's month;
    - with no opening, or for a month that ends at or before the opening, only that month's slot counts: `scheduledSlots`, `upSlots` and `downSlots`, from `figure` without an opening. The result carries `"beforeOpening": true` and no `availability`, `budgetSlots` or `budgetLeftSeconds`.

    § 12 counts the first month from admission opening, so a slot before it is not v2's availability. `figure` with an opening after a month's end would also give a negative budget: an opening on 2026-11-20 gives October −54 budget slots (`standing/availability.py:136-148`). `figure` itself is unchanged.
  - **Refusals.** A refused ledger read prints `{"ok": false, "reason": <its key>}` and exits 1, never a figure without the opening. A word or flag outside the form prints the usage and exits 2.
- [x] (c) **A left-behind scratch is disposed with its receipt (L1-23).** A new recovery word, `remove-scratch {copyId}`, joins `recovery_words.WORDS` and `run_word`; its input is exactly `{copyId}`. It runs `RecoveryProcedures.remove_scratch(copy_id)` (`backend/modules/operations/recovery_procedures.py`):
  - **Before any operation:**
    - an unknown copy is `NOT_FOUND`;
    - a copy that is closed, or not of kind `scratch-restore`, is `CONFLICT` (`not-an-open-scratch`);
    - while any `restore.verify` request is active (`u8_protocols.ACTIVE_RECOVERY`), it is `CONFLICT` (`scratch-in-use`). That set holds a `restore.verify` request still awaiting the operator, running, verifying or unknown (`u8_protocols.py:64-66`). Once no such request remains, the copy is removed even when its verification wrote no RestoreVerification record: an unknown restore that `reconcile` settles `failed` writes none (`recovery_procedures.py:717-726`).

    Step 64(d) records the copy before its restore, so an open copy can also be the scratch of a check still running. A6's busy check (`u8_protocols.py:328-339`) never matches a `restore.verify` request, whose `targetId` is its backup set (`recovery_procedures.py:358`).
  - **The removal.** `u8_protocols.execute_settled(operator, "platform.database.remove", "database-scratch", {"database": <the copy's database>, "via": "in-person"}, key=f"remove-scratch:{copyId}")` runs it. A word run again after a failed removal then runs it under the next retry key instead of replaying the failure, as the migration tool's disposal does (`migration/tool.py:491-519`). A first failure is plausible: the production tool's `DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS`, without `FORCE`, is refused while a session is still connected (`production_tool.py:636-638`). On success it records `RetainedCopies.disposed(copyId, receipt)` and answers `{"copyId", "disposed": true, "receiptId"}`.
  - **Failures:**
    - a `PreconditionRefused` or `ControlError` records `disposal_pending` and answers its reason;
    - an `EffectUnsettled` that is `failed` or `exhausted` does the same, answering `scratch-removal-failed` or `step-retries-exhausted`;
    - an `unknown` outcome answers `effect-outcome-unknown`, and an `in-progress` one `effect-in-progress`. Both leave the copy open without `disposal_pending`.
  - **Why not `remove-database`.** The production tool's `remove-database` stays as built, because it is the effect's own executor (`u8_platform/drivers/arrangement.py:419-426`) and cannot cite a settled receipt: the effect's receipt settles only after it returns, and `disposed` needs a settled receipt (`retained_copies.py:193-211`).

In `scripts/serve_docsuri_u8.py`, `children()` gives the realm's maintenance server `"--log-folder", str(environment.parent / "logs")`, the folder `u8_main.configure_logs` gives the other roles. The existing test `test_each_long_running_job_keeps_alive_and_the_root_jobs_do_not` pins the maintenance job's `ProgramArguments` literally (`test_templates.py:213-215`). Its list gains `'--log-folder', f'{paths.prefix}/profile/logs'` in this step, so operations-1 stays green.
- [x] (c) `backend/maintenance_server.py`, using the standard library only. `backend.log_events` cannot serve here: it imports `backend.local_browser`, and through it psycopg, fastapi and an AccountAccess module (`log_events.py:33`, `local_browser.py:19-27`).
  - **The counts.** `CountedLog(folder, *, clock=…)` keeps `answered`, `refused` and `failed` for the current 5-minute UTC window, under a lock. Its clock defaults to the UTC wall clock. The first window starts at the clock's time floored to 5 minutes, and each next window starts at the previous start plus 5 minutes, so no window is written twice.
    - `flush()` closes every window whose end the clock has reached. Each closed window becomes one JSON line with sorted keys, exactly `{"window": "<the window's start, YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ>", "answered": n, "refused": n, "failed": n}`, appended in order. A window with no request still gets its line.
    - `flush(final=True)`, the exit flush, also closes the open window with its counts so far. A process stopped and started within one window therefore writes two lines for that window, and a reader adds the lines that share a window.
    - A flush that cannot write keeps every line it has not written, in order, and the next flush that can write writes them first. It returns False and prints the fixed key `maintenance-log-unwritable` to standard error. A flush that writes every line returns True.
    - The file is written outside the count lock, one flush at a time, so counting never waits for the disk.
  - **The file.** `CountedLog` writes `<folder>/maintenance.log` through a `logging.handlers.WatchedFileHandler` subclass that is attached to no logger, so no other record reaches the file.
    - It is built with `delay=True`, so nothing is opened until the first flush. A link planted at the name makes flushes fail; it never stops a start.
    - Its `_open` opens the file as `log_events.PrivateWatchedFileHandler._open` does (`O_WRONLY | O_APPEND | O_CREAT | O_NOFOLLOW`, mode 0600), but relative to the log folder's descriptor (`dir_fd`). The folder is opened with `O_RDONLY | O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW`, after it is created at 0700 when it is missing. So nothing is written through a link at the file's name or at the folder.
    - `WatchedFileHandler` reopens the file when the path's device or inode no longer matches its stream. So after the rotation moves the file aside, the next flush creates a new 0600 file, as observability-design § 7 and security-design § 7.3 require of v2's own processes.
    - Its `handleError` re-raises, so a failed open or write reaches `CountedLog`, which catches the `OSError`. Logging's own traceback is never printed.
    - The line's four fields are not among security-design § 7.1's registered fields. The code summary records the correction (Step 104): § 7.1 gains the maintenance server's count line `{window, answered, refused, failed}`, the "own log's counts" of observability-design § 6. The line carries only counts and the window's fixed-form time.
  - **The handler.**
    - `answered`: a 200, or the notice's 503, to GET or HEAD. `refused`: a 405, or any answer `BaseHTTPRequestHandler` sends through `send_error` (400 for a malformed request line, 414, 431, 501, 505).
    - `_send` and the `send_error` override first count the answer's class, before its first byte is written. Building and writing the headers and the body then run in one `try`. If anything there raises, they move that one count to `failed`, set `close_connection` and return without re-raising.
    - Because neither re-raises once it has counted, an exception that reaches the server's `handle_error` comes from a request that was never counted, for example `Pages.answer` raising before `_send`. `handle_error` counts it `failed`, once. It is set on the server instance, with or without a log, and prints nothing. socketserver's default would print the traceback and the client's address to standard error, which is the job's `maintenance.err.log` (D11).
    - The `send_error` override answers with no body, `Content-Length: 0`, the fixed headers with `no-store` (and HSTS when a parsed `Host` is the public authority) and `Connection: close`. A request line parsed as HTTP/0.9 gets no status line and no headers, as in the standard library.
    - `log_message` stays silent.
  - **`MaintenanceServer`** takes `log: CountedLog | None = None`. With None it counts nothing; `maintenance_served` in `test_cutover_journeys.py` and the existing component fixtures build it that way. It still constructs the module's `ThreadingHTTPServer` name, so a test can replace it.
  - **`main()`** requires `--log-folder` and builds `CountedLog(args.log_folder)` on the wall clock.
    - One daemon thread waits on a stop event until the current window's end, then calls `flush()`. A wait that ends early writes nothing, because `flush()` closes only windows whose end the clock has reached, and the thread then waits again.
    - Just before `serve_forever`, `main()` installs SIGTERM and SIGHUP handlers that raise `KeyboardInterrupt` in the main thread, as `docsuri_ops.release.interrupts()` does (`release.py:2145-2160`). It cannot import that function, because the import test admits no `docsuri_*` module. launchd stops a job with SIGTERM and sends SIGKILL after `ExitTimeOut` 30 (`render.py:156-157`), and the realm's `stop_children` sends SIGTERM too (`serve_docsuri_u8.py:217-225`). Without a handler, Python would end at once and lose the open window's counts.
    - When `serve_forever` returns or is interrupted, `main()` restores the earlier handlers, stops the thread, runs `flush(final=True)` and then calls `server_close()`. It returns 0.
- [x] (d) **Where `diskutil` writes a missing volume's line.** `MacTools.volume` and `backup_unlock._info` read only standard output (`isolation_macos.py:120-127, 145-147`; `backup_unlock.py:45-51`), and only recorded output puts `Could not find disk` there today (`operations/test_root_jobs.py:21`). So `/usr/sbin/diskutil info /Volumes/u8-review-no-such-volume` is run once on this Mac through `subprocess.run(..., capture_output=True)`, and code-summary.md records which stream carries the line, and the exit code.
  - If it is standard error, both readers also read standard error when `diskutil info` exits 1, while `MacTools`' other tools keep reading standard output alone. Without that change an absent volume reads as unreadable, and the unlock job records `volume-unreadable` every minute.

- [x] (a) `component/test_maintenance_server.py` (component-2), new test `test_it_listens_on_loopback_only_at_its_two_ports`:
  - A real `MaintenanceServer(Pages.load(build), port=0, …)` binds `'127.0.0.1'`.
  - `backend.maintenance_server.ThreadingHTTPServer` is then replaced by a recorder, so nothing binds 18201 or 18111:
    - it keeps its address and accepts `daemon_threads` and `handle_error`;
    - its `serve_forever` records SIGTERM's and SIGHUP's handlers and returns at once;
    - its `server_close()` records how many lines `logs/maintenance.log` holds when it is called.
  - `main(['--build', build, '--log-folder', logs])` returns 0 and records `('127.0.0.1', 18201)`.
  - With `'--port', '18111'` added, the recorder's `serve_forever` calls the installed SIGTERM handler, `signal.getsignal(signal.SIGTERM)(signal.SIGTERM, None)`. `main` still returns 0 and records `('127.0.0.1', 18111)`.
  - In both runs, the handlers recorded while serving differ from the ones in place before `main`. Once `main` returns, `signal.getsignal` answers the earlier ones, for SIGTERM and for SIGHUP.
  - Each of these raises `SystemExit` and builds no server: `'--port', '18200'`; `'--port', '0'`; `'--port', '3000'`; `'--host', '0.0.0.0'`; a run without `--log-folder`.
  - After the two accepted runs, `logs/maintenance.log` is 0600, and every line in it has zero counts and a window in the form `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ`.
  - `server_close()` was called exactly once per accepted run, each time after that run's exit flush: the line count it recorded is at least 1 at the first call and larger at the second.

  - GET `/` (503);
  - GET `/privacy` (200);
  - GET `/assets/legal-BxtcjqMv.css` (200);
  - HEAD `/terms` (200);
  - POST `/` (405);
  - `BREW / HTTP/1.1` sent raw (501, sent through `send_error`).

  Counting from the raw header list (`getheaders()`, or the raw response for `BREW`), each answer carries each of these exactly once:
  - `Content-Security-Policy` `"default-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'; form-action 'self' https://accounts.google.com https://orcid.org"`;

  - `Referrer-Policy` `no-referrer`;
  - `Permissions-Policy` `camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()`;
  - `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` `same-origin`;
  - `Cache-Control` `no-store`.

  None carries `Set-Cookie`. The set without `Cache-Control` equals `production_boundary.FIXED_HEADERS`. `Strict-Transport-Security` is exactly `max-age=31536000` when `Host` is the public authority, and absent otherwise.
- [x] (c) Same file (component-2), new test `test_failed_requests_are_counted_in_its_own_log`. It runs a server on port 0 with `CountedLog(tmp_path / 'logs', clock=…)`, whose clock starts at 2026-11-01T00:02:30Z. Each client waits for its answer's end or for the connection to close, which comes after the count.
  - **Answered:** GET `/`, GET `/privacy`, GET `/terms?from=footer` and HEAD `/terms`.
  - **Refused:** POST `/` (405) and the raw line `GARBAGE` (400). The server parses that line as HTTP/0.9, so the client sees only the connection closing.
  - **Failed:** a second server on the same log uses a `Pages` stand-in.
    - For `/raises`, its `answer` raises, and the client sees the connection close without an answer (`http.client.RemoteDisconnected`).
    - For `/unwritable`, it answers 200 with a body that has a length but no buffer interface, so `wfile.write` raises once the headers are sent. The client reads the 200 and then `http.client.IncompleteRead`.
    - `capfd`'s standard error stays empty: no traceback, no client address.
  - **The flushes:**
    - At 00:05:00Z, `flush()` returns True and writes exactly one line, whose object is `{'window': '2026-11-01T00:00:00Z', 'answered': 4, 'refused': 2, 'failed': 2}`. The unwritable answer is counted once, as failed, and not as answered.
    - The file is 0600. It holds no path, query, `Host` value or method: none of `/privacy`, `/terms`, `from=footer`, `/raises`, `/unwritable`, `127.0.0.1:18111`, `GET`, `HEAD`, `POST` or `GARBAGE`.
    - At 00:10:00Z, the next flush writes `{'window': '2026-11-01T00:05:00Z', 'answered': 0, 'refused': 0, 'failed': 0}`.
    - `maintenance.log` is then renamed `maintenance.log.20261101`. The flush at 00:15:00Z creates a new 0600 `maintenance.log`, with another inode, holding only the 00:10:00Z window. The moved file keeps its two lines.
  - **Links.** Each case uses its own `CountedLog` over its own folder, with a clock starting at 00:02:30Z; building it opens nothing.
    - With `maintenance.log` a link to an outside file, `flush()` at 00:05:00Z returns False, the outside file keeps its bytes, and standard error holds exactly the line `maintenance-log-unwritable`. Once the link is removed, `flush()` at 00:10:00Z returns True, and the new 0600 file holds the kept 00:00:00Z line, then the 00:05:00Z line.
    - With the log folder itself a link to an outside folder, `flush()` returns False, nothing is created in the outside folder, and standard error holds exactly the line `maintenance-log-unwritable`.

### Step 83 — API / endpoint: a recovery request from an open incident and the assistance history's bound — implement

- [x] (a) L1-19 (fix it now), in one ledger step (L1-64). `backend/modules/operations/http.py` `submit()` (http.py:145-169), with `RecoveryRequests.request` in `recovery.py` (recovery.py:168-205) and the incident's versions in `incidents.py` (incidents.py:130-161).
  - The problem today: the request is recorded first (http.py:155-164), then `link_recovery` refuses an incident that is still `open` (incidents.py:154-161). 운영 offers 복구 요청 on every unresolved incident (incident-list.tsx:74), so a request from an open incident answers `409 CONFLICT` and leaves the request unlinked.
  - The fix: `submit()` keeps its policy and revision checks (http.py:146-151), and `RecoveryRequests.request` still checks the origin and the second factor before it takes the ledger's lock (recovery.py:172, 145-158). Its one `Ledger.atomic` step then checks the request as built (recovery.py:183-190) and the named incident together, and appends with `_LockedView.append_all` (ledger.py:757-775), in L1-19's order:
    1. the incident's `investigating` version, with `diagnosisKey` `recovery-requested` (the key fits the ledger's `KEY` form, ledger_records.py:165);
    2. the new request, `requested`, naming the incident;
    3. the incident's `recovering` version, with the request linked.

    That is the order the ServiceIncident machine gives (open → investigating → recovering; ledger_records.py:307-311). An incident already `investigating` or `recovering` gets only the third version.
  - The code: `RecoveryRequests.request` gains `incidents=None`. Given an `Incidents` and an `incident_id`, its step also appends the incident's versions. Without them it records the request alone, as built: the schedule's requests are unchanged, and Step 89(c)'s restore request still links through `link_recovery`. `Incidents` gains `recovery_versions(view, incident_id, request_id)`, which reads the incident through the locked view and returns its versions with their expected revisions, appending nothing. `begin_diagnosis` and `link_recovery` keep their answers and share its two version rules (incidents.py:146-161). `submit()` passes its `incidents` (http.py:111) and no longer calls `incidents.get` or `link_recovery` itself (http.py:153-154, 161-164).
  - Any refusal writes nothing: the step makes every check before it appends, and `append_all` checks every version on a trial copy of the fold before it writes any. The refusals are a stale `expectedRevision` or a reused `submissionId` (`409 CONFLICT`), a restore naming a set the ledger does not hold or an incident that does not exist (`404 NOT_FOUND`), and a second factor that is no longer current (`403 FORBIDDEN`, refused before the step). The incident then stays `open`, and 운영 still offers 복구 요청 on it.
  - An incident resolved between 운영's list and the request is refused with `409 CONFLICT` before any request exists, so a 409 never leaves a recorded request behind.
  - A replay of the same submission recovers its request first, as built (recovery.py:183-185), and appends nothing: no incident version and no second request, even once the incident has moved on or resolved.
  - The module docstrings of `http.py`, `recovery.py` and `incidents.py` say so.
  - 운영 shows the key as the evidence `diagnosis:recovery-requested` (dashboard.py:355-356), which IncidentList prints raw today as '진단: recovery-requested' (incident-list.tsx:54). Step 93(f) gives it Korean copy, '진단: 복구 요청됨'.
  - No contract changes: `OpsRecoverySubmissionHttp` already carries `incidentId`. Tested in Step 89(b).
